item.text: {"text":"RSS defines recency by interaction position within the supplied chronological sequence, rather than elapsed time. Its exponential importance is f(k)=α^(n−k), 0<α≤1, normalized into target-sampling probabilities p(k)=f(k)/Σf(j). It draws c≈τn target positions with replacement, removes selected targets from the input, and predicts them as multiple positives from the remaining ordered subsequence. Thus RSS changes both targets and context; it does not simply choose contiguous training windows or multiply next-item losses by recency weights. Recency operates through target selection; BCE or LambdaRank supplies the training loss. GRU4Rec is among the evaluated backbones. [RSS paper, §§4.1–4.3](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/299238/2/299238.pdf)\n\nMathematical comparison: normalized exponential per-position weighting, Σk w(k)ℓk, equals the expected loss of sampling one position with probability w(k) only when contexts and component losses remain fixed. RSS removes sampled targets and uses multiple positives, so this equivalence does not establish equivalence to RSS. For a contiguous window ending at b, normalized exponential weights satisfy α^(b−k)/Σwindow α^(b−j)=α^(N−k)/Σwindow α^(N−j): resetting the endpoint cancels algebraically within that window. Nevertheless, random-window coverage and separate normalization determine overall interaction influence; an old window still receives its allocated training weight. Truncation excludes older targets entirely. Consequently, RSS supports positional recency bias as prior art, but does not directly validate window-normalized next-item loss weighting or establish its novelty. Those are deductions from the objectives, not experimental findings reported by RSS."}
